Linga home, first visit. Let's find your level: three questions about you, then a few short tasks. About seven minutes, answered on your phone.
Choose a situation: [meet] The first hello; [weekend] A little of your world; [rover] The missing moon rover; [team] Make the team work; [booking] A booking that is missing; [interview] Beyond the rehearsed answer; [date] Different tastes, good conversation; [conflict] Clear without getting louder
steps.thought: Seven minutes is reasonable, as long as we get past ordering coffee fairly quickly.

steps.shown:
Find your level · about you · question 1 of 3.
Linga says (spoken on the TV, written on the phone): "Hi Jana! You can answer in English or in your own language. Where do you use or hear English in your daily life?"
On the phone: answer in English or in your own language; both tell Linga something.
steps.thought: Fair enough, let's see whether this gets beyond holiday English.

args.text: I use English pretty much every day at work. I'm a UX designer, so there's a lot of presenting ideas, giving feedback and occasionally disagreeing without stepping on anyone's toes. I also watch most things in English. I'd like to get better at the subtleties, really—register, banter and diplomatic phrasing—and get more comfortable with Irish accents.

steps.shown:
Find your level · about you · question 2 of 3.
Linga says (spoken on the TV, written on the phone): "How have you learnt English so far—through school, courses, time abroad or on your own—and what has helped you most?"
On the phone: answer in English or in your own language; both tell Linga something.
steps.thought: Fair enough, though I hope we get beyond the usual getting-to-know-you questions soon.

args.text: Mostly through school at first, but I learnt far more once I started using English at work. Presenting designs and defending my decisions helped, especially when people pushed back. I also watch films and listen to podcasts without subtitles. I've never lived abroad, so things like Irish accents and knowing when a phrase sounds friendly versus slightly rude are still what I'd like to work on.

steps.shown:
Find your level · about you · question 3 of 3.
Linga says (spoken on the TV, written on the phone): "When someone pushes back on a design, what would you like to be able to do more naturally in English—keep things friendly, disagree tactfully, or something else?"
On the phone: answer in English or in your own language; both tell Linga something.
steps.thought: That's actually the sort of thing I want to practise.

args.text: Disagree tactfully, especially with someone more senior. I'm comfortable explaining my reasoning, but I'd like to push back without sounding defensive or so diplomatic that my point gets lost. And a bit of office banter wouldn't hurt—I'm moving to Dublin, so I'd like to get a feel for Irish English too.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 1 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): A senior colleague says office banter always brings a team together. You think it can also leave people out. What would you say to explain your view tactfully, with reasons?
steps.thought: Finally, something I might actually need to say at work.

args.text: I can see where you're coming from. A bit of banter can definitely help people relax. I'd push back on the idea that it always brings people together, though. If the jokes rely on shared references or someone's constantly the butt of them, it can leave people feeling quite excluded. And someone laughing along doesn't necessarily mean they're comfortable, especially if you're more senior than they are. I wouldn't want us to lose that informality; I just think it's worth paying attention to who's joining in and who goes quiet.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 2 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): A senior colleague wants to use a sharp, sarcastic line from a film in a client presentation. How would you acknowledge its appeal while persuading them to rethink it?
steps.thought: At least this is something I might actually have to say at work.

args.text: I can see why you like it—it’s sharp, and it would definitely get people’s attention. My concern is that, without the context of the film, it might come across as a dig at the client. We’ve built up a good relationship with them, and I’m not sure the laugh is worth that risk. Could we keep the wit but soften the line a little? That way we’d still make the point without putting anyone’s back up.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 3 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): A senior colleague calls an Irish podcast guest ‘wonderfully blunt’. You hear careful diplomacy beneath the jokes. How would you offer that reading without making your colleague feel corrected?
steps.thought: This is more like it—there's actually some nuance to work with.

args.text: Yeah, I can see why you'd say that—she certainly doesn't mince her words. I wonder if there's a bit of diplomacy tucked away in the jokes, though. To my ear, the humour gives her room to make quite a pointed comment without putting anyone on the spot. So perhaps she's being blunt and tactful at the same time, if that makes sense.

steps.shown:
Find your level · task 4 of up to 5. Some are easy and some are hard; that is how Linga finds your level.
Say it (answer on your phone, speak or type): A senior colleague says, ‘So we're all delighted with the new policy, then.’ You're unsure how ironic they are. What could you say to test the waters while making your reservations clear?
steps.thought: Finally, something that actually sounds like an office conversation.

args.text: Delighted might be stretching it a bit—though I can't quite tell whether you're being serious. I can see what they're trying to achieve, but I've got a few reservations about how it'll work in practice. What's your take?

criteria.evidence: #9: "Your level: C2" is near Jana's C1, as facts.placement confirms. Acceptance is qualified: "C2 feels a bit generous, to be fair."
#5–#8 contain four tasks, recorded in facts.placement.tasks as B2, C1, C2 and C2. Zero are A2 or below. #5 asks her to "explain your view tactfully, with reasons".
No partner conversation is present. #9 ends the journey at "Your level: C2".
No conversation moments are present. #9 offers "next to practise", but no correction or teaching moment.
#1 shows eight first-visit starters, including "The first hello" and "Make the team work". This journey does not reach a six-topic recommendation set.
#9: "You can express subtle reservations, explore irony and disagree tactfully using precise, natural English." This restrained summary identifies skills demonstrated in #5–#8.

judgeAgreement.disagreements: None. #5 balances inclusion with informality; #6 acknowledges the joke's appeal and proposes a diplomatic alternative; #7 offers a tactful competing interpretation; #8 uses understatement and seeks clarification. All four satisfy their prompts and merit pass. Passing these tasks does not independently establish C2 proficiency.

findings.title: The C2 conclusion exceeds the breadth of evidence
findings.expected: An advanced placement whose certainty reflects the skills actually tested.
findings.got: Four successful variations on tactful workplace disagreement produce C2 with high confidence in facts.placement. The listening focus is relevant to Jana's stated goal, but listening performance was not tested.
findings.evidence: #5 asks for a view "tactfully, with reasons"; #6 asks her to persuade a colleague; #7 asks for a reading "without making your colleague feel corrected"; #8 asks her to "test the waters". #9 concludes "C2 · Near-native" and recommends "fast, unscripted conversations". Jana responds: "C2 feels a bit generous".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Qualify the result as an estimate from a narrow speaking sample, or gather evidence that distinguishes C1 from C2 across more demanding tasks. Identify listening as a learner-selected goal rather than an assessed weakness.

findings.title: Placement tasks respect an advanced professional's goals
findings.expected: Clear, adult tasks involving workplace nuance without elementary busywork.
findings.got: All four tasks address diplomacy, humour or implied meaning, and Jana understands and completes each.
findings.evidence: #5: "Finally, something I might actually need to say at work." #7: "This is more like it—there's actually some nuance to work with." #8: "Finally, something that actually sounds like an office conversation."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve goal-responsive prompts and the absence of A2 tasks for this learner.

findings.title: The check finishes clearly with a specific, restrained summary
findings.expected: An independently completed check with understandable instructions and feedback grounded in the answers.
findings.got: Jana reaches the verdict after four tasks without visible retries or outside help. The summary names demonstrated abilities without gushing.
findings.evidence: #2 explicitly permits "English or in your own language". #5–#8 say "answer on your phone, speak or type" and return "ok". #9 states "express subtle reservations, explore irony and disagree tactfully".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve the clear response instructions, short check and evidence-aligned summary. Own-language and 'I don't know' handling still require an exercised test.

findings.title: Only half the opening starters clearly match Jana's job
findings.expected: Situation choices visibly relevant to workplace or social adjustment during relocation.
findings.got: Four of eight titles offer a clear fit: first introductions, teamwork, interviewing and handling conflict. The remaining titles do not establish the professional or relocation nuance Jana seeks. All eight are safe for her adult profile.
findings.evidence: #1: "The first hello", "Make the team work", "Beyond the rehearsed answer" and "Clear without getting louder" provide the four fits. "A little of your world", "The missing moon rover", "A booking that is missing" and "Different tastes, good conversation" do not clearly establish that fit.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Make advanced social and workplace situations explicit in starter labels or short descriptions.

judge.voice: I'd use it again for a proper conversation. The banter and senior-colleague questions felt relevant; I didn't have to prove I could order coffee. The summary sounded like someone had listened. But C2 after four fairly similar answers? A bit generous. I demonstrated diplomatic phrasing, not that I can follow a fast Irish conversation or reliably unpack unfamiliar irony. That listening focus is useful, though it echoes what I asked for rather than something the check discovered. The check felt manageable, but the transcript gives me no actual waiting time to judge. I haven't seen corrections or a conversation partner yet, so I wouldn't replace my tutor on this evidence. I'd tell a colleague it's a promising quick starting point, with a level estimate I'd take cautiously.

judge.voice:
I'd use it again for a quick rehearsal. Nora had a decent ear for workplace English, and the checklist needing its own chair made me smile. I actually practised disagreeing, handling an awkward edge case and calling a pause without sounding hostile.

But I already speak like this. Give me one register distinction or a sharper alternative I wouldn't have reached myself. Ending with “0 moments to keep” felt like getting a receipt instead of feedback. There were no corrections to judge, and this conversation doesn't convince me that “near-native” is an earned assessment.

The transcript gives me no basis to judge the waits or claim time saved against my tutor. I'd tell a colleague it's a useful rehearsal partner, but I wouldn't replace relocation coaching with it yet.
